People assume compliance exists to catch people doing the wrong thing, and after eleven years in this job I would say the opposite is closer to the truth. A rule exists so that the person at the front does not have to be brave on their own. If there is no written limit, then every no is personal: the customer thinks you decided, and next season he remembers it. If there is a limit, the answer is not about you at all. You can say I am not allowed to approve that at this level, and it is true, and nobody has to lose face. That is why I get irritated when somebody calls a procedure bureaucracy. Sometimes it is. But most of the time the procedure is the only thing standing between an analyst and a very uncomfortable telephone call. The one thing I would say to anybody new is this: you must know exactly what you can authorize yourself, because the moment you are not sure, you start apologizing, and once you start apologizing the customer knows the door is open.

I say no about four times a week, and I have learned that the words have to change completely depending on who is in front of me. With a family farm I have known for twenty years, I do not hide behind the policy. I say it plainly, I explain what I can do instead, and I usually say it on the telephone rather than in writing, because a letter to that man would feel like a threat. With a large distributor, it is the reverse. There, everything goes in writing, everything names the clause, and I use the formal words on purpose: we are not able to authorize an increase at this stage. That is not coldness. In a big company the person reading my email has to forward it to somebody else, and if my message is warm and vague it is useless to them. The mistake I made for years was having one register for everybody. I was too formal with the small customers, who found me distant, and too casual with the big ones, who found me unserious.
